outcome: Design key and certificate lifecycle controls, trust validation, and recovery while identifying the authority and evidence for each critical transition.

sections.body: Key lifecycle includes generation, registration or binding, storage, distribution, activation, use, rotation, suspension or revocation, backup or recovery where authorized, archival, and destruction. Separate key custodianship, application administration, and approval duties where risk warrants it. Protect key material with scoped access and suitable hardware or service boundaries, record usage, define compromise response, and test restoration. A recovery process must not become an undocumented key-export path.
keyPoints: A key is an access-enabling asset with its own classification and owner.
Rotation, revocation, and recovery need tested triggers and accountable authority.
sections.title: Control every key lifecycle transition

sections.body: PKI establishes and operates a chain of trust that binds an identity or service to a public key through issuance and validation processes. A relying party must validate the certificate or assertion according to its intended use, trust anchors, validity period, names or identities, policy constraints, and available revocation or status mechanism. Issuance quality matters: a certificate is not trustworthy merely because it has a cryptographic signature; the enrollment, identity proofing, authorization, and CA protection must support the intended reliance.
keyPoints: Certificate validation is a runtime decision, not only a procurement choice.
Trust anchors and issuance authority define the scope of a PKI claim.
sections.title: Validate identity-to-key bindings

sections.body: For compromised keys or certificates, identify authority to suspend or revoke, distribute status, rotate dependent services, notify relying parties, preserve required evidence, and restore secure operation. Build inventories that connect keys and certificates to systems, owners, data, dependencies, and expiry. Test expiry, lost key, CA or service outage, and emergency replacement paths. Availability pressure must not lead to bypassing validation permanently; use a documented, risk-owned exception and a plan to remove it.
keyPoints: Inventory and dependency mapping make cryptographic incidents recoverable.
A PKI outage is both an availability event and a trust-validation decision.
sections.title: Plan compromise, continuity, and evidence

summary: Keys and certificates create operational trust paths: generation, protection, access, issuance, binding, distribution, validation, rotation, revocation, recovery, archival, and destruction. An architecture is only as strong as the authorities and evidence governing those lifecycle transitions.

learningJob.plainExplanation: After compromise, authorized owners must scope the event, publish status, contain trust, replace keys and certificates, and verify relying parties. A status outage needs a preapproved bounded fail policy rather than permanent validation bypass.

workedExamples.reasoning: Define trusted issuers, workload enrollment and identity proofing, private-key protection, service name validation, expiry and revocation response, log evidence, and an emergency rotation procedure. Test that an expired or wrong-name certificate fails safely and that replacement does not grant extra authorization.
